paras: The bombing of 4660 Prairie Avenue was an attack on an apartment building in Chicago, Illinois, into which a Black family, "the only Negro family in the block," was moving in the summer of 1920. A bomb exploded beneath the front stairway before the family had finished moving in, demolishing the front of the building but injuring no one. The only account found is a short item in the Colorado Statesman, which headlined it as a bombing "by whites."

According to the Colorado Statesman of August 7, 1920, the family moved into an apartment at 4660 Prairie Avenue, where no other Black family lived on the block. "Before all of their furniture was in," a bomb was set off beneath the building's front stairway. The blast demolished the front of the building and shattered windows in other apartments within a radius of 300 feet, but no one was injured. The report gives no date, so the bombing can only be placed on or before the August 7 issue.
The item names neither the family nor any suspect, and no report of an arrest or investigation appears in the coverage.

The Colorado Statesman, a Black weekly, ran the story on its front page as a three-sentence brief under the headline "Colored Family Is Greeted With a Bomb by Whites." The headline supplied the attribution to white bombers, while the text itself stated only what happened to the building. No white-press report of the bombing was found.

reader.title: Bombing of 4660 Prairie Avenue
bases: The only report describes a bomb exploded beneath the front stairway of an apartment building into which a Black family was moving, damaging property and injuring no one (A1).

Only the Colorado Statesman's brief item (A1) describes the Prairie Avenue bombing; the Chicago Whip items of August 14 (A2-A4) concern a different bombing at 440 E. 48th St., and no white-press report was found.

accounts.label: Black press news brief
accounts.gist: A Chicago item said a bomb exploded beneath the front stairway as the only Negro family in the block moved into 4660 Prairie Avenue, demolishing the building front and shattering windows within 300 feet, with no one injured.

framing.detail: The Colorado Statesman's headline 'Colored Family Is Greeted With a Bomb by Whites' cast the bombing as a white attack on a Black family moving into a white block; the text itself is a flat factual report.

record_check.dossier: No date is given; the item ran August 7, 1920, so the bombing occurred on or before that date and may have been in late July.
Unidentified; the headline attributes the bomb to 'whites' (initiator white per headline only).
One Black paper (Colorado Statesman) reports this bombing; the Chicago Whip caption is for the 440 E. 48th St. bombing, and the Cleveland Advocate editorial does not mention it.
Not stated in the report; follows from the Chicago dateline.

sources.note: Only account: bomb exploded beneath front stairway as the only Negro family in the block moved into 4660 Prairie Avenue, Chicago; no one hurt, building front demolished.
quotes: The only Negro family in the block moved into an apartment at 4660 Prairie Avenue. Before all of their furniture was in, a bomb was exploded beneath the front stairway.
There was no one injured, but the front of the building was demolished and windows in other apartments within a radius of 300 feet were shattered.

set_aside: Photo caption of 'Chicago's latest "race hate" bombing'; its wording matches the Whip's page-1 story on the 440 E. 48th St. bombing (A3, A4), not Prairie Avenue.
Bomb thrown from a Ford car at 440 E. 48th St., home of Mr. and Mrs. J. Jackson, on a Sunday night; watchman fired on the car. Separate bombing.
Continuation of A3: only windows broken on 48th Pl.; blames inactivity of Cook County law enforcement.
Editorial on Ohio primaries and Northern discrimination; names Chicago among cities that 'staged race riots', not this bombing.
